title: Prove It: Find the Groups
goal: I can find the groups in a word problem and write the number sentence.

card.desc: Bristol proves this week's skill on harder word problems. She hunts for clue words (each, every, per), spots in all traps that are really addition, writes the number sentence, and sees that arrays are equal groups in rows and that 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 have the same total.

win: You proved it! You can find the groups in any story.

slides.title: On Your Own: Find the Groups
slides.text: You did this in class. Now show what you can do. 🔍

slides.title: Think about your book
slides.text: Read each question. Tell a grown-up your answer.
prompts: Which girl in the Critter Club is most like you? Why?
What is one thing Amy does to look for the missing puppy?

items.q: Pond A has 5 frogs. Pond B has 5. Pond C has 3. Are the groups equal? Type equal or not equal.
items.why: Pond C has only 3. The groups are not equal.
items.no: Look at pond C. Does it have 5?

items.q: There are 5 vases. Each vase has 2 roses. How many roses?
items.no: Each vase has 2. Skip count by 2s five times.

slides.title: Your detective tools
slides.text: Clue words: each, every, per. They mean equal groups.
slides.tip: In all can mean add or multiply. Look for the clue word!

slides.title: Groups and each
slides.text: Ellie has 5 bags. There are 10 beads in every bag.

items.q: How many groups?
items.why: The bags are the groups. There are 5 bags.
items.no: What holds the beads? Count those.

items.q: How many beads in each group?
items.no: Read the sentence with every. How many beads are in one bag?

items.q: How many beads in all?
items.no: Skip count by 10s, one time for each bag.

slides.title: Multiply or add?
slides.text: Tap a card. Then tap the right box.

items.text: Amy has 4 jars. Each jar has 10 buttons.
Marion has 4 red pens and 10 blue pens.
items.hint: Is there a clue word? Is 4 the same as 10?

items.text: There are 3 dogs. Every dog has 4 legs.
items.hint: Does every dog have the same number?

items.text: Ellie read 5 pages on Monday and 3 pages on Tuesday.
items.hint: Did she read the same number each day?

items.text: The shelter gives 2 walks per dog. There are 5 dogs.
Amy has 2 kittens. Liz has 5 kittens.
items.hint: Do they have the same number?

slides.done: Clue word and same size → multiply. Different sizes → add.

items.q: This array has 3 rows of 10. How many sunflowers?
items.no: Skip count by 10s, one time for each row.

items.q: Which number sentence matches this array?
no: An array is equal groups. Multiply, don't add.
Count the rows again. There are 5.

slides.title: Goldfish bowls
slides.text: Ellie has 4 fish bowls. There are 2 goldfish in every bowl. Make the groups.
slides.hint: The bowls are the groups. How many fish in each bowl?

items.q: 2 rows of 5 make 10. How many are in 5 rows of 2?
items.why: Turn-around facts have the same total: 5 × 2 = 10.
items.no: Turning an array does not add or take away any.

items.why: Turn-around facts have the same total: 3 × 10 = 30.
items.no: It is the same two numbers, turned around.

slides.title: Word problems
slides.text: Find the clue word. Then decide.

items.q: Liz has 3 jars. There are 5 treats per jar. Do you multiply or add? Type multiply or add.
items.why: Per jar means each jar has 5. Equal groups: 3 × 5 = 15.

items.q: Amy has 3 bones. Marion has 5 bones. How many bones in all?
items.why: 3 and 5 are not equal groups. Add: 3 + 5 = 8.
items.no: Is there a clue word? Are the groups the same size?

items.q: Which story matches 2 × 5?
choices: There are 2 dogs and 5 cats.
There are 5 dogs. 2 dogs go home.
There are 2 dogs. Each dog has 5 toys.
no: 2 dogs and 5 cats are not equal groups. That is 2 + 5.
Dogs going home is take away: 5 − 2.

sets.q: The shelter has 2 kennels. There are 8 kittens in every kennel. How many kittens?
sets.no: Every kennel has 8. That is 2 groups of 8.

sets.q: Ellie has 5 goldfish and 3 turtles. How many pets in all?
sets.why: 5 and 3 are not equal groups. Add: 5 + 3 = 8.
no: 15 is 5 × 3. There are not 5 groups of 3 here.
2 is 5 − 3. Nothing was taken away.

sets.q: Which number sentence matches this array?
no: Count the rows again. There are 5.
An array is equal groups. Multiply, don't add.

sets.q: 4 rows of 6 chairs make 24 chairs. How many chairs are in 6 rows of 4?
sets.why: It is the turn-around fact. The total stays the same: 6 × 4 = 24.
sets.no: Turning the rows does not add or take away chairs.

sets.q: Which story matches 4 × 5?
choices: Amy has 4 bones. She gets 5 more.
There are 4 dogs. Each dog has 5 spots.
There are 4 dogs and 5 cats.
no: She gets 5 more. That is adding: 4 + 5.
4 dogs and 5 cats are not equal groups. That is 4 + 5.

sets.q: Liz walks 5 dogs every day for 3 days. How many dog walks is that?
sets.no: The days are the groups. How many walks each day?

sets.q: Marion has 10 pens. Liz has 3 pens. To find how many in all, do you multiply or add? Type multiply or add.
sets.why: 10 and 3 are not equal groups, so add: 10 + 3 = 13.
sets.no: Is there a clue word? Is 10 the same as 3?

sets.q: A garden has 4 rows. Every row has 10 carrots. How many carrots?
no: 14 is 4 + 10. Every row has 10. Count all 4 rows.
30 is only 3 rows. Count all 4 rows.

sets.q: The pet store has 5 cages. There are 2 hamsters per cage. How many hamsters?
sets.no: Per means each. Skip count by 2s, one time for each cage.

sets.q: Amy found 10 shells. Ellie found 4 shells. How many shells in all?
sets.why: 10 and 4 are not equal groups. Add: 10 + 4 = 14.
sets.no: Is there a clue word? Are the groups the same size?

sets.q: Which number sentence matches these carrots?
no: An array is equal groups. Multiply, don't add.
Count the rows again. There are 2.

sets.q: 5 rows of 3 make 15. How many are in 3 rows of 5?
sets.why: Turn-around facts have the same total: 3 × 5 = 15.
sets.no: Turning the rows does not change the total.

sets.q: Which story matches 3 × 5?
choices: There are 3 boats and 5 ducks.
There are 5 ducks. 3 ducks swim away.
There are 3 boats. Each boat has 5 ducks.
no: 3 boats and 5 ducks are not equal groups. That is 3 + 5.
Ducks swimming away is take away: 5 − 3.

sets.q: There are 4 tables. Each table has 2 cups. How many groups are there?
sets.why: The tables are the groups. There are 4 tables.
sets.no: What holds the cups? Count those.

sets.q: Which word problem needs add?
choices: There are 5 bikes with 2 wheels per bike.
Liz has 5 red beads and 2 blue beads. How many beads?
There are 2 boxes with 5 pens in each box.
sets.why: 5 red and 2 blue are not equal groups, so add: 5 + 2 = 7.
no: Each bike has 2 wheels. That is equal groups.
Each box has 5 pens. That is equal groups.

sets.q: Marion has 3 pockets. She has 10 coins in each pocket. How many coins?
sets.no: Skip count by 10s, one time for each pocket.

sets.q: The vet has 3 rabbits. She gives 10 carrots per rabbit. How many carrots?
sets.no: The rabbits are the groups. How many carrots does each rabbit get?

sets.q: Liz saw 2 birds in the morning and 10 birds at night. How many birds in all?
sets.why: 2 and 10 are not equal groups. Add: 2 + 10 = 12.
no: 20 is 2 × 10. There are not 2 groups of 10 here.
8 is 10 − 2. Nothing was taken away.

sets.q: How many puppies are in this array?
sets.no: Count the rows. Count one row. Then skip count, one time for each row.

sets.q: 2 × 9 = 18. Which fact has the same total?
sets.why: Turn-around facts have the same total: 9 × 2 = 18.
no: 9 + 2 is adding. A turn-around fact is still multiplying.
2 × 2 is 4. A turn-around swaps the two numbers.

sets.q: There are 10 apples on each of the 5 trees. How many groups are there?
sets.why: The trees are the groups. There are 5 trees.
sets.no: What holds the apples? Count those.

sets.q: Ellie has 5 cats. Amy has 5 cats. Liz has 4 cats. Are the groups equal? Type equal or not equal.
sets.why: Liz has only 4. The groups are not equal.
sets.no: Does every girl have the same number of cats?

sets.q: Which story matches 5 × 10?
choices: There are 5 boxes. Every box has 10 crayons.
There are 10 crayons and 5 pens.
There are 10 crayons. Amy uses 5.
no: 10 crayons and 5 pens are not equal groups. That is 10 + 5.
Amy uses 5. That is take away: 10 − 5.

sets.q: Amy has 2 bags of food. Each bag has 5 cans. How many cans?
no: 7 is 2 + 5. Each bag has 5. Count both bags.
3 is 5 − 2. Nothing was taken away.

practice.intro: Three tries on each one. Only your first try counts. Look for the clue words: each, every, per. Watch out for traps!

questions.q: There are 2 plates. Each plate has 6 strawberries. How many strawberries?
questions.no: Each plate has 6. Count 6, then 6 more.

questions.q: Ellie has 6 cat toys and 2 dog toys. How many toys in all?
questions.why: 6 and 2 are not equal groups. Add: 6 + 2 = 8.
questions.no: Is there a clue word? Are the groups the same size?

questions.q: How many puppies are in this array?
questions.no: Count the rows. Skip count by 5s.

questions.why: Turn-around facts have the same total: 2 × 8 = 16.
questions.no: It is the same two numbers, turned around.

questions.q: There are 3 kennels. Each kennel has 4 dogs. Which tells the number of groups?
choices: 3 kennels
4 dogs
12 dogs
questions.why: The kennels are the groups. There are 3.
no: 4 is how many dogs are in each kennel.
12 is all the dogs, not the groups.

questions.q: The pet store puts 2 toys per cage. There are 6 cages. Which number sentence fits?
questions.why: Per cage means each cage gets 2. 6 groups of 2: 6 × 2 = 12.
no: Every cage gets 2 toys, so the groups are equal. Multiply.
There are 6 cages, not 2.

questions.q: Amy saw 5 puppies on Monday and 10 puppies on Tuesday. How many puppies in all?
questions.why: 5 and 10 are not equal groups. Add: 5 + 10 = 15.
questions.no: That is the trap! Are the groups the same size?

no: An array is equal groups. Multiply, don't add.
Count the rows again. There are 4.

choices: There are 4 bikes. Every bike has 2 wheels.
There are 3 boxes with 10 crayons in each.
Liz has 2 dogs and 4 cats.
questions.why: 2 dogs and 4 cats are different amounts.
no: Every bike has 2 wheels. Those groups are equal.
Each box has 10. Those groups are equal.

questions.q: Marion has 5 pockets. She has 5 coins in every pocket. How many coins?
questions.no: Skip count by 5s, one time for each pocket.

questions.q: One array has 2 rows of 9. Another has 9 rows of 2. Which is true?
choices: 2 rows of 9 has more
9 rows of 2 has more
They have the same number
questions.why: 2 × 9 = 18 and 9 × 2 = 18. Turn-around facts are the same!
no: Count them both. 2 × 9 = 18 and 9 × 2 = 18.
Count them both. 9 × 2 = 18 and 2 × 9 = 18.

1. There are 4 kennels. Each kennel has 2 puppies. How many puppies?

2. The vet gives 3 treats per dog. There are 5 dogs. How many treats?
___ groups of ___    ___ × ___ = ___
3. Ellie has 5 red leashes and 4 blue leashes. How many leashes in all?
4. There are 3 bowls. Every bowl has 10 kibbles. How many kibbles in all?
5. Liz has 2 hamsters and 6 fish. How many pets in all?

pages.directions: Draw each array. Then write the number sentence.

items.text: 6. Draw 2 rows. Put 5 dots in each row.
7. Now turn it: draw 5 rows with 2 dots in each row.
8. Array 6 has ______ dots. Array 7 has ______ dots. Circle one:
9. Write a word problem for 3 × 5.

pages.title: Part 5: Book corner
pages.directions: Use a capital letter and a period.

items.text: 10. Tell what happened first and next in your book.

teacher.objective: Bristol proves the Week 1 skill on harder word problems: she finds the groups using clue words (each, every, per), rejects "in all" traps that are addition, writes the matching number sentence, reads arrays as equal groups in rows, and uses turn-around facts (3 × 4 = 4 × 3).
materials: 6 index cards: write the 6 sort cards from class slide 7. Also bring her 2 story cards from Lesson 1.
A highlighter or colored pencil for clue words
A sheet of paper to turn the bean array (class slide 11)
Her book, Amy and the Missing Puppy
Printed packet (2 pages) to send home

plan.do: Class slides 1–2. State today's goal. She names the big problem and retells 3 events with first, next, then. Push for complete sentences.

Class slide 3. She reads her 2 story cards from Tuesday and says multiply or add for each. Then she says equal or not equal and why, and types it. If she has not passed Lesson 1's check, redo the bean cups first.
Class slides 4–5. Write the kitten story on the whiteboard; she highlights every. Then 3 cages of 2 beans: she types groups, each and total.

plan.block: The "in all" trap and card sort
plan.do: Class slides 6–8. Bunny story under the kitten story: no clue word, so add. Then the 6 index cards into Multiply and Add piles, saying the clue word for each, and the two trap items.
Class slides 9–12. She builds 3 rows of 5 and skip counts. Then 3 rows of 4 on paper, turns the paper, counts 4 rows of 3. Ask: did the total change?
Class slides 13–15. Fish tanks, the 5 detective steps, then 3 stories read aloud; she writes each number sentence on the whiteboard before you click.
Class slide 16. She reads every choice aloud and names the groups and the number in each.
Class slide 17. Open the course page and read the task list. Tonight: the after-class lesson (it ends with Show What You Know). Practice, packet and reading are due before Monday's Zoom lesson.

watch: Multiplying any time she sees "in all" (for example 4 × 3 for 4 big bunnies and 3 baby bunnies). Ask: is there an each, every or per? Are the groups the same size?
Swapping groups and the number in each (writing 2 × 3 for 3 cages with 2 in each). Say: the groups come first. Point to the cages.
Counting an array's columns as rows. Have her slide a finger across ➡️ for each row.
Thinking a turn-around fact gives a new answer. Build both arrays with beans and count.

packet_key.answer: 10 and 10. Circle Same (turn-around facts have the same total).
Any story with 3 equal groups of 5 that uses the word each, for example: There are 3 cats. Each cat has 5 toys. (3 × 5 = 15)
Two complete sentences about the book in order (first, next) with capital letters and periods.

teacher.notes: Show What You Know is now at the end of the after-class lesson, done on her own tonight. She needs 85 (7 of 8). A retake gives her a brand-new set of 8 questions (3 sets rotate), so she cannot memorize answers. If she is still under 85 by Monday, ask a parent to set out about 30 beans, redo the clue-word highlighting and the bean arrays at the start of Monday's lesson, then have her retake before the new lesson. Watch item 9 in the packet: if her story has unequal groups, she has not yet got the idea.

tasks: Thursday night: do the After-class lesson. Finish Show What You Know (get 85).
Friday: do the Lesson 2 Practice. Try to get 85 or more.
Friday: do page 2 of the Lesson 1 Packet (the page you saved).
Saturday: do page 1 of the Lesson 2 Packet.
Sunday: do page 2 of the Lesson 2 Packet.
Saturday or Sunday: do the reading lesson Pathways Week 8 Reading: Mia Steps Up. Read the story carefully and use clues from the text. Aim for 85. If it is locked, type 1111.
Every day: read your book for 15 minutes. Be ready to tell what happened.

slides.title: Prove It: Find the Groups
slides.text: Today you prove what you know. 🔍 You will find the groups hiding in the words.

notes.do: Before she sits down, set out: about 40 beans, the 6 index cards for the sort (class slide 7), whiteboard and marker, a highlighter, her book.
notes.say: Today is Prove It day. On Tuesday you learned that equal groups mean multiply. Today you find the groups that hide inside the words of a story.
notes.listen: Every group has the same number. If she says "groups that are big," show 3 cups of 2 beans next to cups of 2, 2, 5.

slides.title: Tell me about your book
slides.text: Think about Amy and the Missing Puppy.
prompts: What is the big problem in the story?
What would you do next if you were Amy?
starters: If I were Amy, I would …

notes.do: 5–6 minutes. She answers out loud in full sentences. Tap the gold button for each strong answer.
notes.ask: What is the big problem? Tell me 3 things that happened, in order. What would you do next if you were Amy?
notes.listen: A clear problem (Ms. Sullivan's puppy, Rufus, is missing, and Amy wants to find him), three events with first, next, then. Push for a reason on the last prompt: "I would … because …"

slides.title: From Tuesday
slides.text: Equal groups → multiply. Not equal → add.

items.q: Look at the groups. Are they equal? Type equal or not equal.
items.why: Two groups have 5. The last group has only 4. So they are not equal.
items.no: Count every group. Do they all have the same number?

items.q: There are 2 trays. Each tray has 10 muffins. Do you multiply or add? Type multiply or add.
items.why: Each tray has 10, so the groups are equal: 2 × 10 = 20.
items.no: Find the clue word. Is every tray the same?

items.q: Marion found 6 acorns. Amy found 9 acorns. How many acorns?
items.why: 6 and 9 are not equal groups, so add: 6 + 9 = 15.
no: 54 is 6 × 9. There are not 6 groups of 9 here.
3 is 9 − 6. Nobody lost any acorns.

notes.do: First she reads her 2 story cards from Tuesday and says multiply or add for each one. Then she says each answer below out loud and why, then types or taps it herself.
notes.ask: How do you know they are not equal? What word tells you the trays are equal?
notes.listen: "The last group has only 4." "Each tray has 10." On the acorns, 54 means she multiplied the two numbers she saw: ask, "Are there 6 groups of 9?"

slides.title: Clue words: each, every, per
slides.text: These words tell you the groups are equal.

visual.sub: They all mean: the same in every group

steps.text: Read: There are 5 kittens. Every kitten has 2 bows.
How many groups? 5 kittens. How many in each? 2 bows.

slides.tip: The number of groups comes first. The number in each group comes second.

notes.do: Write the kitten story on the whiteboard. She highlights every. Then click through the steps.
notes.say: These three words are clue words. Each, every and per all tell you every group has the same number.
notes.ask: Which number is the groups? Which number is in each group?
notes.listen: 5 kittens are the groups, 2 bows in each. If she says 2 groups of 5, have her point to one kitten and count its bows.

slides.title: Find the groups
slides.text: The vet has 3 cages. There are 2 puppies in each cage.

items.q: How many groups are there?
items.why: The cages are the groups. There are 3 cages.
items.no: Count the cages. The cages hold the puppies.

items.q: How many puppies are in each group?
items.no: Read the sentence with each. How many puppies are in one cage?

items.q: 3 groups of 2 = ____ puppies.

notes.do: Draw 3 cages on the whiteboard. She puts 2 beans in each cage before she types.
notes.ask: Point to one group. How many are in it?
notes.listen: Groups = 3 (cages), each = 2. If she types 2 for the groups, she took the number of puppies. Ask: "What holds the puppies?"

slides.title: Watch out for the trap!
slides.text: In all means find the total. It does not always mean multiply.

steps.text: Read: Liz has 4 big bunnies and 3 baby bunnies. How many bunnies in all?
Is there a clue word like each? No. 4 and 3 are not equal groups.

slides.tip: Ask: are the groups the same size? Then pick multiply or add.

notes.do: Write the bunny story under the kitten story. She looks for a clue word and finds none.
notes.say: In all means find the total. It does not tell you to multiply. You still have to check: are the groups the same size?
notes.ask: Is there an each, every or per? Are 4 and 3 the same?
notes.listen: "No clue word, and 4 is not 3, so add." If she says 4 × 3, build 4 beans and 3 beans side by side.

slides.title: Trap or not?
slides.text: Look closely. Some cards have the same numbers! Tap a card. Then tap the right box.

items.text: Ellie has 3 cats. Each cat has 2 bows. How many bows in all?
items.hint: Find the clue word. Does every cat have 2?

items.text: Liz has 3 cats and 2 dogs. How many pets in all?
items.why: 3 cats and 2 dogs are not equal groups: 3 + 2 = 5.
items.hint: Is there a clue word like each? Are 3 and 2 the same?

items.text: There are 5 rows of tulips with 10 in every row.
items.hint: Does every row have the same number?

items.text: Amy saw 10 dogs in the morning and 5 dogs after lunch.
items.hint: Did she see the same number both times?

items.text: The vet gives 2 pills per day for 5 days.
Marion has 2 red leashes and 5 blue leashes.
items.hint: Are there 2 red and 2 blue? Look again.

slides.done: Clue word and same size → multiply. Different sizes → add.

notes.do: Lay the 6 index cards face up. She reads one, says the clue word (or "no clue word"), puts it in a Multiply pile or an Add pile, then taps it on screen.
notes.say: Some cards use the same numbers. The numbers do not decide. The words decide.
notes.ask: This card has a 3 and a 2. So does that one. Why does one multiply and one add?
notes.listen: "Each cat has 2 bows" (equal) versus "3 cats and 2 dogs" (not equal). If she sorts by the numbers, cover the numbers with a finger and reread.

items.q: Amy has 2 bags of dog food and 5 cans of dog food. How many bags and cans in all?
items.why: This is the trap! 2 and 5 are not equal groups, so add: 2 + 5 = 7.
no: There are not 2 groups of 5. There are 2 bags and 5 cans.
Nothing was taken away.

items.q: Each of the 4 girls brings 5 treats to the shelter. How many treats?
items.why: Each girl brings 5. That is 4 groups of 5: 4 × 5 = 20.
items.no: Every girl brings 5. Skip count by 5s, one time for each girl.

notes.ask: Is this one a trap? How do you know?
notes.listen: Bags and cans: no clue word, 2 and 5 are different, so add (7). Girls: each girl brings 5, so 4 × 5 = 20. If she types 9, she added the girls to one girl's treats.

slides.title: Arrays are equal groups
slides.text: An array has rows. Every row has the same number.

steps.text: Count the rows: 3 rows. (A row goes across ➡️.)

slides.tip: Each row is one equal group.

notes.do: She builds 3 rows of 5 beans on the table, then skip counts 5, 10, 15 while sliding a finger across each row.
notes.say: An array is equal groups lined up in rows. Each row is one group.
notes.ask: How many rows? How many in each row?
notes.listen: 3 rows, 5 in each. If she counts down the columns, have her slide a finger across ➡️ for each row.

items.q: Which number sentence matches this array?
no: 2 + 6 adds the number of rows to one row. Count all the flowers.
There are only 2 rows, not 6.

items.q: How many bones are in this array?
items.no: Count the rows. Then skip count by 5s, one time for each row.

notes.ask: Say the rows first, then how many in each row.
notes.listen: "2 rows of 6, 2 × 6 = 12" and "4 rows of 5 is 20." If she types 9 for the bones, she added the number of rows (4) to the number in one row (5). Have her skip count 5, 10, 15, 20, one count per row.

slides.title: Turn-around facts
slides.text: Turn an array on its side. The total stays the same!
slides.tip: If you know one fact, you know its turn-around too!

notes.do: She builds 3 rows of 4 beans on a sheet of paper. Then she turns the paper a quarter turn and counts 4 rows of 3.
notes.say: We did not add any beans. We did not take any away. We only turned the paper.
notes.ask: Did the total change when we turned it?
notes.listen: "No, it is still 12." If she wants to count again, let her: that is the proof.

items.q: 3 rows of 5 make 15. How many are in 5 rows of 3?
items.why: Turn-around facts have the same total: 5 × 3 = 15.
items.no: Turn the array. Did any beans go away?

items.q: Which is the turn-around fact for 2 × 10?
no: 2 + 10 is adding. A turn-around fact is still multiplying.
10 × 10 is 100. A turn-around swaps the two numbers.

notes.ask: What is the turn-around fact? Is the total the same?
notes.listen: "5 rows of 3 is still 15." On the second item, 10 × 10 means she thinks turn-around changes a number. Show 2 rows of 10 beans and turn the paper.

slides.title: The pet store fish
slides.text: The pet store has 5 fish tanks. There are 3 fish in every tank. Make the groups.
slides.hint: The tanks are the groups. How many fish are in each tank?

notes.do: She says "5 groups, 3 in each" before you click the buttons together. Then she makes the 5 tanks with beans.
notes.ask: Which number is the groups? How did you know?
notes.listen: "The tanks are the groups." Total 15 (skip count 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 or 5, 10, 15).

slides.title: Detective steps
slides.text: How do you solve a word problem? Tap the steps in order.
steps: Find the groups and how many in each.
Check: skip count or draw it.
slides.why: Read, find, choose, write, check. Use these steps every time!
slides.hint: Not that one yet. Another step comes before it.

notes.say: This is your detective routine. Use it on every word problem, in class and in your packet.
notes.ask: Why do we read the whole problem first?
notes.listen: "So we know what is happening before we pick." If she starts with "multiply," remind her that we choose only after we find the groups.

slides.title: Write the number sentence
slides.text: Listen to each story. Write the number sentence on the whiteboard.

steps.text: Story 1: Marion has 2 baskets. Every basket has 9 eggs.
Story 2: Liz picked 10 apples. Ellie picked 2 apples. How many apples in all?
Story 3: The vet gives 2 baths per dog. There are 10 dogs.

slides.tip: Groups first, then how many in each.

notes.do: Read each story out loud before you click. She writes on the whiteboard, then you click to show the answer and she checks her own work.
notes.ask: Equal or not? Which operation? Which number is the groups?
notes.listen: Story 3 is the hard one: the groups (10 dogs) come at the end. If she writes 2 × 10, say: "The total is right. Which number is the groups?" Both totals are 20, but she should name the dogs as the groups.

items.q: Which story matches 3 × 10?
choices: Liz has 3 shells and 10 rocks.
There are 3 vans. Each van has 10 kids.
There are 10 kids. 3 kids go home.
no: 3 shells and 10 rocks are not equal groups. That is 3 + 10.
Kids going home is take away: 10 − 3.

items.q: All three say in all. Which one is the trap where you add?
choices: There are 4 nests with 2 birds in each. How many birds in all?
Ellie has 4 birds and 2 fish. How many pets in all?
There are 2 cages with 4 birds in every cage. How many birds in all?
items.why: 4 birds and 2 fish are not equal groups: 4 + 2 = 6.
no: This one says each. It is 4 groups of 2, so you multiply.
This one says every. It is 2 groups of 4, so you multiply.
